name: Curiosity
intro: Curiosity is a car-sized rover that landed in Gale crater on 6 August 2012. It found that an ancient lake there could have supported microbes. It is still working today, climbing Mount Sharp and reading its rock layers like a history book.
whyLeft: It has not been left: Curiosity is still exploring. Like every Mars rover, it was always meant to stay on Mars for good.
repurpose: It is still doing its job. Its wheels are wearing out on sharp rocks, so the team plans gentler routes and sent new driving software that slows the damage.

hotspots.title: The laser mast
hotspots.text: The cameras on this mast see Mars in colour, and a laser called ChemCam zaps rocks up to 7 meters away to find out what they are made of.

hotspots.title: Worn wheels
hotspots.text: Curiosity’s thin aluminium wheels have holes and cracks from sharp rocks. A scout would check them closely: they still roll, and new driving software from 2017 adjusts each wheel’s speed to slow the damage.

photo.alt: Close-up of a metal rover wheel with dents and torn holes.
photo.caption: Holes and dents in Curiosity’s left-front wheel, photographed by the camera on its own arm in 2013.

hotspots.title: Nuclear power
hotspots.text: Curiosity’s power comes from the heat of decaying plutonium in this box at its back. That is why dust storms and winter cannot switch it off the way they did solar-powered rovers.

hotspots.title: The drill
hotspots.text: The drill on the end of this arm powders rock for the labs inside. In 2013 the first drilled rock showed that Gale crater once held a lake with water that microbes could have lived in.

hotspots.title: The landing camera
hotspots.text: A small camera under the rover’s body filmed the landing. You can watch the heat shield fall away and the ground rush up before a rocket-powered sky crane lowered Curiosity onto its wheels.

video.caption: Curiosity’s own landing camera: the heat shield falls away and the ground of Gale crater rushes up. Real footage, no sound.

funFact: Holes in Curiosity’s wheels spell “JPL” in Morse code, so it stamps the letters into the Martian ground as it drives.
